en: The Ritual Procedures for Making Offerings to the Devas,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Shijia at Baoliang Forest Monastery in Guangzhou.

This single method for offering to the devas originally derives from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* and is performed during the time of practicing repentance, wherein offerings are set forth for the Triple Gem and the various devas.
However, at the site of the almsgiving (*dāna-kṣetra*), one should only install the seat of Puṇyadevatā to the left of the Buddha.

If the ritual site is extensive, further install the seats of Mahāprajñā and the Four Heavenly Kings to the right of the Buddha. According to the new sutras, one should have images of these deities painted.

At the time of the invitation, the order of precedence for host and guest and their respective ranks must be observed; next, one invites the eight classes of beings as a whole, and finally, one makes the three requests.
Regarding Puṇyadharā (Gongde Tian): one recites the celestial mantra seven times to summon the goddess and her retinue, for this deity is the presiding master of the Dharma-gate of the *bodhimaṇḍa*.
The ancient masters enumerated sixteen celestial deities; later, the Sun, the Moon, and the Dragon King were added.
Yama was originally the twentieth; nowadays, people have increased this to twenty-four. Since there are no assigned seats, the proper order is lost.
When inviting deities during the performance of repentance rituals, there are established protocols within the ritual manuals themselves.

Although we are not currently performing a repentance ritual but merely making offerings, one must still know the hierarchy of their positions. Regarding their conduct and speech, Mahāpratibhāna possesses great merit.

Venerable One, when the Master of the Treatise leads the rite, Brahmā and Śakra are placed first. However, according to the ritual for repentance (*chánfǎ*), the presiding lord (*zūnzhǔ*) should take precedence.

Furthermore, upon examining both the new and old sūtras, one must additionally invite the Eight Divisions (*bābù*), including even the deities of wind, fire, and water, to accord with the intent of the scriptures.
In this [text], wind and the others are not listed separately because they belong to the Eight Divisions; by inviting the Eight Divisions, they are already included.
Although those within the intermediate state do not engage in formal debate, they all gather at the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* assembly;
they delight in the Mahāyāna and propagate the True Dharma, performing great work in its protection. As the Dharma Master Shen Huan once said: "When people of the world discuss the heavens..."
They may be twelve, sixteen, or eighteen, all increasing or decreasing according to the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits" without fixed restriction.
Now, if one wishes to establish a hierarchy of honor and subordination, it is likewise difficult to do so with certainty. For instance, Kārttikeya (Gizi-mu) is a rākṣasa;
how could he be ranked as an equal to Mahābrahmā? He has a daughter named Guṇakāra and a son named Vajrapāṇi (Sanji). Now, some place Guṇakāra [at the head].
Above [are the Brahmās], followed by Śakra; then the list concludes with Vaiśravaṇa and the Mother of Ghosts—is this not a violation of the proper order?

Consequently, I have examined the Tripitaka and composed biographies of the various devas, explaining them according to their respective ranks. Generally, among the devas there are hosts and guests, males and females, original and manifested forms, and the manifest and the hidden.
Brahmā is the lord of the three realms; Śakra is the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; and the Four Kings are...
Regarding the eight classes of spirits: as for Guṇakara and Mahāmati, they are merely sojourners. Guṇakara resides in Northern India, while Mahāmati dwells in the mountains and marshes;
neither has ever had a presiding lord. This is what is meant by "host and guest. [The others are] Guṇakara, Mahāmati, and the tree deity.
The Earth Deity, Mārīcī, and the Mother of Ghosts are all female in essence; the others are male in form, which refers to their being male and female respectively.
Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada and his five hundred followers are all originally great bodhisattvas; they manifest in divine positions as their traces.
This refers to what are called the "fundamental" (hon) and the "traced" (saku). When Mahāpratibhāna addressed the Buddha, he was fit to propagate the True Dharma;
although his rank was that of a guest and his body manifested as female, his words and deeds were manifest. Or, one may act merely as a shadow or echo and not engage in propagation;
even if one possesses authority as a ruler and manifests in a male form, one's words and deeds may remain obscure. This is what is meant by "manifestation and obscurity. One who understands this—

The Ritual Declaration (Kneeling on the right knee, declare:)

I reverently contemplate that the Tathāgata, while governing the world, does not depart from the fundamental limit (*dharmadhātu*). Yet his transformation reaches throughout the three thousandfold great chiliocosm;

appearing according to the capacities of beings to benefit them, he establishes teachings of five vehicles and ten vehicles. Adorned with meditative concentration and wisdom, he manifests bodies for self-enjoyment and for the enjoyment of others.

His radiance shines everywhere, accomplishing benefits that moisten both the hidden and the manifest. With a single voice he expounds the Dharma, so that all may attain it according to their own needs.

He is the compassionate father of the four modes of birth and the sole sovereign of the nine realms. When the conditions for his response arise through the resonance of sentient beings' capacity, he answers them as surely as an echo.

Thus, within the assembly of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings were revealed together, bringing benefit and inspiration to devas and nāgas, and bestowing peace and joy upon boundless multitudes.

A modest cause. Beholding now the bequeathed instructions of the Great Hero (Mahāvīra), I respectfully adhere to the holy teachings and reverently present this humble offering of aquatic plants (*pingyi*).

"With single-minded devotion, I reverently invite the World-Honored One, Vairocana-Muni, who does not depart from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) yet appears for the sake of all living beings;

V. Invoking the Devas (The five groups of monastics do not kneel when invoking the devas; only laypeople should prostrate. Holding the incense burner, they should say:

she is called the One of Great Eloquence (*Mahāprajñā*) because she bestows the wondrous wisdom of *dhāraṇī*; and she is known as the one who manifests supernatural powers and protects the True Dharma. This is...
Vajrapāṇi, having been promoted to the heavens of the First Dhyāna, was appointed as the lord of the Sahā world and titled the Great Brahmā King.
Residing at the summit of the Form Realm, he governs the great trichiliocosm; therefore, he is called Maheśvara (The Great Sovereign).

Lord Śakra dwells in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, specifically presiding over the authority of the lower realms. The Four Heavenly Kings reside within the belly of Mount Sumeru, commanding the deities of the Eight Divisions.
They benefit all beings through vast transformation, protecting the Dharma and bringing peace to the Sangha. Among them, General Vajrapāṇi is foremost;
thus, among the holy assembly of the *Prabhāsa-samādhi* assembly, there are none who do not manifest through the skillful means revealed in the Vaipulya scriptures.

With sincere devotion, we establish this vow to protect the Dharma and bring peace to all beings. This shall not only provide support during the present age, but specifically serve to sustain the Dharma during the final era.

We humbly pray that you will fully manifest your divine power to assist in propagating the True Teaching, and that you will silently observe the sentiments of sentient beings to joyfully accept this morning’s offering. [Name], the donor.

This humble offering (if one is a renunciant, adjust the title according to their precepts). May it secretly draw forth Your sacred gaze and look down with compassion, taking pity on the sincere devotion of all living beings.
We look up to You, hoping for universal deliverance from the perilous straits of delusion, so that we may soon fulfill our hearts' desire and attain liberation.
Therefore, with utmost sincerity and single-minded devotion, we take refuge in You.

With all reverence and single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions. (After one prostration, recite: I extend these words:
The Triple Gem is the most excellent field of merit and source of blessing;
Mahābrahmā, Lord of the Sahā World, and Maheśvara, Lord of the Great Trichiliocosm;
Śakra, the Four Kings, and the earth-dwelling devas— Possessing auspicious merit and great renown, these sages are able to bestow fortune, wisdom, and eloquence.

the Bodhi-tree deity and the Joyful Mother— may the eight classes of beings, including devas, nāgas, and asuras,

These fragrant flowers of mine pervade the ten directions, forming subtle and wondrous towers of light.
There are celestial music and divine precious incense; celestial delicacies and divine precious garments.
These inconceivable particles of the sublime Dharma—within each single particle, all particles emerge.

may those who receive this perfuming all give rise to the Bodhi-mind, together enter the state of non-arising, and realize Buddha-wisdom. (At this point, scatter flowers with the hands. If not scattering them, visualize flowers descending from the void. Then, hold up the incense burner and say:)
May these clouds of incense and flowers pervade the realms of the ten directions,
making offerings to all Buddhas, the Honored Dharma, and the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas;
may they arise as platforms of radiant light for all celestial beings and immortals, extending beyond boundless regions throughout infinite Buddha-lands.
Performing the Buddha’s work, Universally perfuming all sentient beings, May they all resolve upon Bodhicitta.

If it is winter, the offering should still be made at the beginning of the fourth watch (*chen*). Having made the offering, one praises it as follows:

The Buddha’s compassion is vast and pervasive; his power and virtue are profound and deep. May the various devas who protect the world bring forth sweet rain, so that calamities and obstacles shall never again invade.
I pray you will deign to examine this humble offering; may blessings and wisdom converge here in abundance.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dhyānaratnagarbha (Recite three times).

[If one does not recite the Buddha’s name, make vows, and dedicate the merit, then recite the Verses on the Extraordinary Practice for Offering to the Buddhas and Feeding the Devas. After completing the Three Refuges, if one wishes to recite [the following], it should be done as follows:]
○ Dedication and Aspiration through the Eight Recollections of the Buddha (First, recite the verses in praise of the Buddha from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*):
The Buddha’s face is like the pure full moon, And like a thousand suns emitting radiance;
His eyes are pure, long, and wide like blue lotuses, His teeth are white, even, and closely set like jade or snow.
The Buddha’s virtues are boundless like the great ocean, Within which infinite, wondrous jewels are amassed;
The waters of wisdom and virtue are ever full, And hundreds of thousands of supreme concentrations completely fill it.
The wheels upon his soles are all exquisitely adorned, With hubs, rims, and a thousand spokes, all perfectly even.
With webbed hands and feet, perfectly adorned, Possessing the marks like the king of swans;
The Buddha’s body blazes like a mountain of gold, Pure, extraordinary, and peerless.
Like Mount Sumeru, replete with merit, I bow my head to the King of Buddha-mountains.
The marks and signs are like space, unfathomable; Surpassing a thousand moons, they radiate light like flames and illusions— Inconceivable!

Therefore, I bow my head with a mind free from attachment. (Having finished the praise, recite: *Note: The "recitation" (*chengyun*) refers to the specific liturgical verses or mantras to be chanted following the verse of praise.*
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha, the Great Teacher of the three realms, the compassionate father of the four modes of birth, the Master of gods and humans in the Sahā world,
who manifests a thousand billion transformation bodies.
Namo Śākyamuni Buddha (Recite as many times as desired. Then perform the usual vows, dedication of merit, prostrations, and the threefold refuge).

In the past, when people made offerings to the devas, they frequently experienced miraculous responses. This was truly because they followed the Dharma with utmost sincerity and maintained purity and reverence both internally and externally.

They prepared altars in clean locations—whether in a saṃghārāma, an araṇya, or some secluded and tranquil place, or within halls, palaces, or towers—and purified the ground, sweeping the four walls, sprinkling scented water, and further smearing them with fragrant mud.
It remains most excellent to prepare peaceful and pure offerings—bowls, basins, vases, and vessels that have never been used—and to adorn the various seats.
Upon these seats, one should scatter exquisite flowers, spread powdered incense, burn various famous incenses, and provide pure lamps and candles.

Only by inclining the heart and exhausting one’s intent can one truly move the deities. Recently, I have observed that when monks and laypeople make offerings to the heavens, their hearts lack sincerity.

This is grave. If the site is not solemn and pure, the ritual implements are not new, and the food and drink are not refined—merely following worldly custom while hoping for the response of the sages—is this even possible?
Since one neither attracts the worthy nor moves the sages, it is truly a hollow exercise.
To claim that one's prayers have yielded no results while incurring the fault of slander—who can take responsibility for such sin? Once the external appearance is pure, one must furthermore...
To purify the three internal karmas: bathing with fragrant water and wearing clean garments is called the purification of bodily karma (*kāyakarma*).

Refraining from idle speech and rinsing the mouth with willow twigs is the purification of verbal karma (*vākkarma*). Focusing the mind with diligent reverence so that mindfulness is not distracted is the purification of mental karma (*manaskarma*).
When these three karmas are thus pure and reverent, there is nothing that will not be received [by the deities].
The devas were displeased. Although their bodies were bathed, they did not maintain ritual purity; thus, they had not yet attained what is truly good and beautiful.

This refers to the washing and cleansing of the hands. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "If, after voiding excrement or urine, one does not wash and cleanse the hands according to the Dharma, one should not circumambulate the stūpa, walk the path of practice, pay homage to the Buddha, or recite the sūtras. The devas will not be pleased."
The methods for reciting mantras will all be without efficacy. If one performs vegetarian offerings, copies scriptures, or fashions images, the merit obtained will be meager;
such constitutes the conduct of the lowest class and shall lead to rebirth in the evil realms. As the Buddha has taught, how can one not be cautious?
The methods for cleansing after using the toilet are detailed elsewhere.

Śikhin Mahābrahmā-rāja. "Brahmā" is the Sanskrit term;

in the language of Fan (Chinese), it means "Pure. This refers to the Heavenly King who purely maintains the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*), whose majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) is without deficiency, and whose body and mind [are likewise pure].

Sublime and perfect, further endowed with clear awakening, he dwells between the heavens of the first and second dhyānas of the Form Realm, presiding over the Brahma assembly and serving as the lord of the Sahā world. Śikhin—translated into Chinese as "Crest"—[reigns] within the trichiliocosm.

There are ten billion Brahmā kings. The Brahmā king in this location is named Śikhin; because he dwells within the great trichiliocosm and acts as its sovereign ruler, he is called the Great Brahmā King.
His body is one and a half yojanas in height, and his lifespan is one and a half kalpas.
This is based on sixty small kalpas constituting one and a half kalpas; it is not a great kalpa (mahākalpa). There are [four] great kalpas in total.
For eighty minor kalpas, the Sūtra says that the devas of the form realm descend to listen to the Dharma.
Sixty devas sit together upon the tip of a single needle, yet there is no crowding; they do not obstruct one another at all.
This is because their physical bodies are so subtle that they are like the lights of various lamps, which interpenetrate one another and reach everywhere without any hindrance. They...
It is also like this. Śakra Devānām Indra in the Sanskrit language;
in the Chinese language, it means "Capable Lord of Devas. This refers to his ability to serve as the lord of the Thirty-three Heavens.
Now, he is briefly called Śakra. He manifests with a thousand heads and a thousand eyes, holding a vajra from which flames of fire issue forth.
He dwells upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, within the great city of Sudarśana. In its center is a golden city containing a most excellent palace.
This palace measures one thousand five hundred yojanas in circumference and is fully adorned with various kinds of wondrous jewels.

It outshines the celestial palaces; therefore, it is named "Excellence" (Vaijayanta). In the center of the palace is a multi-storied circular chamber, thirty yojanas in width, ninety yojanas in circumference, and forty-five yojanas in height.

This is the dwelling place of Śakra, composed entirely of lapis lazuli and inlaid with various jewels. One hundred years in the human realm [is equivalent to one day and night] in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Their day and night constitutes one day for those with a lifespan of one thousand years. Calculated by human days and months, this equals three hundred and sixty million years.
In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the height of the gods is two and a half *li*; the body of Śakra, King of Devas, is five *li*. He has two great crown princes:
the first named Candana and the second named Supīla. Furthermore, there are ninety billion nayutas [of attendants].
The heavenly maiden also has a thousand sons and immeasurable ministers as her retinue.
Śakra shall come to attain Buddhahood, and his name shall be the Honored One Without Attachment (Vimala-guru). In the past, when he was a human being, his clan name was Kauśika;
together with thirty-two companions, he jointly repaired the stupa of Kāśyapa Buddha. By virtue of this merit, he was rewarded with the position of Lord of Devas. [Thirty-two...]
Humans serve as ministers [to the gods], and together they are called the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa). In Sanskrit, it is *Trāyastriṃśa*; in this language, it means "thirty-three.
One *yojana* is forty *li*. A *nayuta* is here translated as ten billion (*wan yi*).
In the north is Vaiśravaṇa Deva-rāja;
"Vaiśravaṇa" in Sanskrit means "Much-Hearing" (Duowen) in the Chinese language. His father’s name was Varuṇa, and his mother’s name was Vasudharā.
This deity’s merit and fame are most preeminent. He dwells upon the northern crystal terrace halfway up Mount Sumeru. There are three...

The city has three names: first, Bhīṣaṇa (The Terrifying); second, Devapūjita (Honored by Gods); and third, Gaṇāśraya (Abode of the Multitude). It governs immeasurable yakṣas and rākṣasas and protects the northern quarter.
The Buddha commanded him to take charge of and support the stupa containing the relics of the ancient Buddhas. [The artist] wished to paint his image.

As stated in the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha*: "Adorned with various celestial garments of exquisite beauty, he stands with his left hand holding a spear planted in the ground, while his right hand, bent at the elbow, supports a Buddhist stūpa."

The Heavenly King of the East, Dhṛtarāṣṭra—Dhṛtarāṣṭra in Sanskrit, meaning "Holder of the Nation" (Chíguó) in the Flower-Ornament Language—refers to one who is able to protect and sustain the land. His father’s name was Nanda;
his mother’s name was Mṛgī. He dwells upon the eastern golden terrace of Mount Sumeru, at its midpoint, in a city named Uttara.
The worthy one presides over the hosts of gandharvas and piśācas and guards the eastern direction. His image is adorned with celestial garments as described previously;
his left arm is extended downward holding a sword, while his right arm is bent forward with the palm facing upward.
A jewel is held in his palm, from which light radiates. *Piśāca*—in the language of China, this means a "demon that devours vital essence.
To the south is the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka;
*Virūḍhaka*—in the language of China, this means "Increase"—meaning he is able to cause the increase of one's own and others' majestic virtue and roots of goodness.
His father’s name was Viśākha; his mother’s name was Ulūpī. He resided on the southern sapphire terrace halfway up Mount Sumeru.
His city was named Sudarśana, and he ruled over the kumbhāṇḍas, the pūtanas, and immeasurable spirits.
He guards the southern direction. His image is adorned with celestial garments; his left hand is as described before, and his right hand holds a spear, the base of which touches the ground.
*Kumbhāṇḍa*—in the language of China, this means "demon-possessing ghost. *Pretas*—in the language of China, this means "hungry ghosts."
The Western Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa—Vaiśravaṇa means "various speech" in the language of China, signifying that he is able to produce all kinds of speech; he is also called "Broad Eyes."
Because his eyes are vast and wide, his father’s name is Parāga and his mother’s name is Ukkiṭī.
He dwells on the western silver terrace halfway up Mount Sumeru; his city is named Cūla.
He rules over the Pūtanas and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nāgas, guarding the western direction. His image is adorned with celestial garments; his left hand is as described before. His...
Holding a red cord in their right hands, these Four Kings are the first heaven of the Desire Realm and serve as the lords of the eight classes of beings.
Fifty human years constitute one day and night for this heaven; their lifespan is five hundred such years. Calculated by human days and months, this equals nine million years.
They are all born by transformation, and their height is five *li* plus one-fifth. As for the Four Kings of old...
Upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, they all realized the first fruit of enlightenment (*srotāpatti*).
Each had ninety-one sons, handsome in appearance and all named "Emperor" (*Ti*). They possessed great majestic power and protected the ten directions.
Each king had eight generals who traversed the three worlds to guard the Buddha’s disciples, as well as all mountains, rivers, trees, lands, cities, and fortresses, including all the spirits therein.
□. All are under the jurisdiction of the Four Heavenly Kings. A new sutra states:

The Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, we four kings, together with the twenty-eight yakṣa generals and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yakṣas, shall use our pure divine eyes—which surpass those of worldly men—to observe and protect this Jambudvīpa. World-Honored One..."
For this reason, we kings shall each act as protectors against the *pūtana*— the Chinese term for which means "stench-ghost" (*chou egui*)—
also known as the "ghost that presides over fever" (*zhushu bing gui*).
The Vajra Secret Lord, the Great General Ratnacandra:
this deity holds a vajra in his hand and has mastered all the secret deeds of the Tathāgata; thus he is named.
"Ratnacandra" is his title. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "In the past, there was a king whose queen gave birth to..."

There were one thousand sons. Desiring to test the sequence in which they would attain Buddhahood in the future, Krakucchanda drew the first tally, Śākyamuni drew the fourth, and so on until Ruci, who was destined for the thousandth tally.
The second wife gave birth to two sons: one vowed to become a Brahmā King and request his elder brother to turn the wheel of Dharma; the other vowed to become Guhyapada.
Vajradeva protects the teachings of his elder brother and leads five hundred yakṣas, all of whom are great bodhisattvas.
He dwells on the summit of Mount Sumeru and protects the Dharma of the thousand buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa. It is not correct that he is traditionally said to be an emanation of Ruci.
The Heavenly King Maheśvara—*Maheśvara* in the Sanskrit language, translated into Chinese as "Great Sovereign" (*Dà Zìzài*)—is titled Wéilingdì (Emperor of Majestic Spirit).

He has three eyes and eight arms, rides a white ox, and holds a white fly-whisk and a trident. He dwells at the summit of the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*). It is said that he is a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
Sāṃśita manifests as the supreme lord of the Form Realm, presiding over the great trichiliocosm;
his radiance surpasses all others, and he can know the number of raindrops in the great trichiliocosm.
Some consider him to be the sixth heaven of the Desire Realm, while others consider him to be the Great Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna Heaven, but neither is correct. He is the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
His height is sixteen thousand *yojanas*, and his lifespan is sixteen thousand *kalpas*. The *Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha* states:
"I, the Heavenly King Maheśvara, possess sovereign supernatural power. I preside over and govern the kings of ghosts and spirits throughout the trichiliocosm;
I nourish and protect them, and I subdue non-Buddhists and those with false views, causing them all to..."

They submit and take refuge, dwelling securely in the True Dharma. Furthermore, by means of their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they travel through the Buddha-lands of the ten directions to assist the Buddhas in proclaiming the transformation [of sentient beings].
By the power of my divine mantra (*vidyā-mantra*), I manifest bodies within the six realms of existence to deliver and liberate sentient beings.

Internally, I cultivate the pure precepts and practices of a Bodhisattva; having long since entered the stream of the Dharma, I have attained the eighth stage (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*) and am equal in merit.
Accomplishment. Pāpīyān Māra: in the language of the gods (Sanskrit), *māra*;
in the language of China (Chinese), "one who can seize life. He is also able to seize the life of wisdom. He constantly [obstructs] those practicing the Way.
"Pāpīyān" (波旬) means "Evil One" in the language of the Huá (Chinese). This was the name of the Māra-king at the time of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.
He currently resides atop the sixth heaven of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). His palace has seven tiers and measures six thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth.
His body is three li and a half tall, and his lifespan is thirty-two thousand years—equivalent to three thousand two hundred years in the human realm.
One hundred years [on earth] constitutes one day and night for this deity.

Because he formerly practiced as a *brāhmaṇa* and held a great *sarvavidagdha* (unrestricted) almsgiving assembly, his karmic retribution was that of becoming the lord of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Although he is the lord of the desire realm, Śakra performs the work of the Buddha-dharma throughout the four heavens;
even Māra cannot restrain him. Within the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, he also recites mantras to benefit sentient beings. New.

The Sūtra says: The Māra King spoke in verse, saying: "If there are those who uphold this sūtra and are able to subdue all afflictions, such beings as these I shall protect and cause to dwell in peace and happiness. If there are those who preach this sūtra, no māras shall gain access;
by the majestic power of the Buddha, I shall protect them."

The name of the Great General Vaiśravaṇa Yakṣa, in its full Sanskrit form, is Vaiśramaṇa; in the language of China (Huayan), it means "Secret" (Mi). This signifies that his name, conduct, principle, and wisdom are all secret.
He is also called Saṃjñeya, which in the language of China means "Correctly Cognizant. The *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha* states: "The Son of the Ghosts..."
The mother had three sons. The eldest was named Viśvāmitra; the second was named General Saṃjñeya, who held a spear and a trident in his hands;
the third was named Maṇibhadra, who is able to protect all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, removing their afflictions such as grief and distress.
They constantly dwell upon the earth or in the air, each having five hundred followers, leading two...
The eighteen classes of yakṣas and various deities shall, wherever this sūtra is circulated, go together with all the spirits and ghosts to that place to protect the preacher of the Dharma.
Furthermore, they shall bestow their empowerment through the three secrets of body, speech, and mind.
That is to say, by means of the vital essence of various flavors, they shall enter through his pores; this is the empowerment of the secret of the body. [End of] Ornamentation.

To refine his speech and eloquence is the empowerment of the secret of speech (*vāg-guhya*). To cause his mind to advance with courageous vigor is the empowerment of the secret of mind (*manas-guhya*).
Furthermore, it causes those who hear him to enjoy the bliss of humans and devas and swiftly realize *bodhi*. The *New Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* states:
"Having correctly understood, he addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, for what reason is my name "Correctly Understanding" (*Samyagājñā*)?'"
This causal condition was personally realized by the Buddha. I know all phenomena; I am enlightened regarding all phenomena.
In accordance with all phenomena, and as they truly are, I fully understand all their various categories, natures, and distinctions.
I possess the light of inconceivable wisdom; I possess the torch of inconceivable wisdom; I possess inconceivable wisdom.
"O monks, I possess an inconceivable mass of wisdom. I am able to penetrate inconceivable objects;
regarding all phenomena, I have correct knowledge and correct understanding, and I am able to observe them correctly. For these reasons, I am named 'One Who Correctly Understands.'"
For this reason, I am able to cause that teacher who expounds the Dharma to have speech that is eloquent and clearly articulated, fully adorned with excellence;
I also cause vital energy to enter through his pores, so that his physical strength is sufficient, his majestic radiance is courageous and robust, and he achieves inconceivable light of wisdom.
He attains right mindfulness and is free from any retreat or discouragement—all those sentient beings [shall likewise attain these].
Having heard this sutra, one attains the light of inconceivable great wisdom and an immeasurable accumulation of merit.

One shall experience the supreme bliss of humans and devas for immeasurable and innumerable great kalpas, forever leaving the three miserable realms behind, constantly encountering all Buddhas, and swiftly realizing unsurpassed bodhi. Whether man or woman, if one even accepts and upholds this sutra...
Whether one holds a single four-line verse, or a single line, or the title of this King of Sutras,
or the name of a single Tathāgata within this sutra, or the name of a single Bodhisattva— should one resolve to recite these with reverence and make offerings,
I shall protect and sustain them, ensuring they are free from calamities and misfortunes, and that they leave suffering behind to attain happiness.

The Great Goddess of Eloquence (Mahāpratisarā) is so called because she has attained great wisdom and perfected the merit of great eloquence. She dwells either in mountain crags, marshes, or deep recesses;
or she resides in great forests, where she thatches her dwellings with grass and fashions garments from soft grass, her hair bound in a topknot upon her head.

He constantly stands upon one foot and is adorned with eight arms. In his hands he holds a trident, a banner of the sun and moon, a bow and arrow, a sword, a spear, an axe, a lasso, a long mallet, and an iron wheel;
he rings out great bells. Śakra and the various devas constantly offer him worship and praise.
Possessing unimpeded eloquence, at all times he personally protects the world, rescuing beings and benefiting all living creatures.
To circulate the Buddha-dharma: The new sutra states, "If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy,
and disseminate this King of Sutras, and practice according to its teachings, I shall lead my retinue and celestial musicians to come to their location to provide protection,
removing all suffering from illness, malevolent stars, epidemics, evil dreams, and malevolent spirits."
Through the arts of sorcery and the practice of spells, may those who uphold this sutra and all who hear it receive abundant benefit,
so that they may all swiftly cross the great ocean of birth and death and reach non-retrogressive bodhi.

The Great Auspicious Goddess of Merit, the Goddess of Great Merit who accomplishes all matters through her supreme majesty and virtue, planted various roots of goodness in the presence of past Buddhas;
therefore, she has attained a karmic reward of exceptionally sublime appearance and is able to cause the merit and virtue of sentient beings to be fulfilled. New.
The Sūtra says: The Great Auspicious Goddess addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the city of the Northern Heavenly King is named Vasu.
Not far from this city is a garden called Puṣpavicitraśrīprabha. Within it is a magnificent palace made of the seven treasures, where I constantly reside.
I recall that in the past, there was a mountain of lapis lazuli gold, radiant with the light of precious flowers and auspicious."
O Tathāgata Ocean of Auspicious Merit, I have planted various roots of goodness in the presence of that Buddha.
By the majestic spiritual power of that Tathāgata, wherever I direct my thoughts, in whichever direction I look, and in whatever land I arrive,
may I enable immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings to receive all manner of happiness, even down to their every necessity.
The seven treasures, clothing, food and drink, and all necessities of life shall be made fully sufficient.

If one recites this sutra constantly for oneself alone and makes offerings without ceasing, one should universally bestow these merits upon all beings and dedicate them toward Bodhi, vowing to transcend birth and death and swiftly attain liberation. According to the *Dharani-samgraha*, [this concerns] the image of Śrīdevī.
His body is upright and of a reddish-white color. His two arms are depicted with various necklaces, bracelets, armlets, ear-rings, celestial garments, and a jeweled crown.
His left hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), and his right hand performs the mudrā of granting fearlessness through mantra. He sits upon the central platform.

This deity is fully endowed with the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the six supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), equal to a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
There is no difference. It is for the sake of delivering sentient beings that I manifest as a celestial maiden.

Seeing all sentient beings wandering through the six realms of rebirth, submerged in the ocean of suffering, and lacking anyone who awakens them, I now, out of compassion for these sentient beings, wish to protect the goddesses with this divine mantra.

The Heavenly General Weito (韋馱天將) is "Weido" in Chinese, which means "Inspiration. The *Zhilun yaolüe* (Essentials of the Wisdom Treatise) states: The Heavenly General’s surname is Wei and his given name is Kun;
he is one of the eight generals of the Heavenly King of the South and is the leader of the thirty-two generals. He possesses innate wisdom and is sagacious.
He early departed from worldly desires and maintained pure, holy conduct. He cultivated the karma of a perpetual youth (*kumārabhūta*), remaining unstained by celestial desires.

Having received the Buddha’s direct entrustment, he harbored secret practices within while externally protecting the Buddha-Dharma. Governing and defending the three continents, he benefited beings and propagated the transformation [of others], extensively saving all living creatures.
Those whose power on the path was weak were all deluded and disturbed by the sons and daughters of Māra. General [Kṣemadatta] was filled with sorrow...
He hurried forward in alarm. Adapting to circumstances, he eliminated [the obstacles]. There was a matter that required him to go to the abode of the Four Heavenly Kings.
When the kings saw him, they all rose from their seats, addressing him as a general who practices the conduct of a youth (*kumārabhūta*), for the sake of protecting the True Dharma.
The essential nature of the Devī Sthāvarā is indestructible; she is as firm as the Vajra King.

Her merit in benefiting the world is like that of the great earth, which supports and sustains all things and gives rise to the hundred grains and precious treasures. The *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed the Earth...
"O Divine One! This land of Jambudvīpa is entirely protected by you; all that grows upon this earth shall be abundant and sufficient, benefiting all beings.

A new sutra states: The Earth Deity addressed the Buddha, saying, 'World-Honored One, if in future ages there should be kings who expound this sutra, I shall, through my spiritual power, remain at their seats without manifesting my physical form, and I shall bear them upon the crown of my head.'"
Excellent! Having heard this Dharma, my heart is filled with profound joy; my radiance increases, and the essence of the earth is likewise made to flourish.

Even all the lands within the four seas are made fertile and rich; the fields become lush and the soil productive, so that all flowers, fruits, and crops are endowed with perfect color and fragrance. If all sentient beings partake of such a sublime drink as this—
Having eaten, their lifespan, physical vigor, and sensory faculties will be secure; their mental power will be courageous and robust.

Furthermore, whatever is required upon this great earth—including hundreds of thousands of undertakings—will all be fully provided for. The population will flourish, free from all decline and affliction.
If one preaches this King of Sutras for sentient beings— whether it be a single parable, a single chapter, a single past causal account,
the name of a single Tathāgata, the name of a single Bodhisattva, a single four-line verse, or even a single phrase,

down to the title of the work itself— at whatever place it is situated, that ground shall become fertile and rich, surpassing all other places, and cause all sentient beings there to receive [its benefits].
They shall be happy. They shall be excellent in wise giving. Their minds shall be ever firm, and they shall have deep faith in the Triple Gem.

Those who hear this sutra will, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas in future ages, constantly experience supreme bliss among devas and humans, and swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
The Bodhi tree deity, Tianpuduo (Devaputra), spoke in verse, saying: "This deity constantly protects the place where the Tathāgata attained enlightenment;
thus, the Bodhi tree is named after it. He himself declared regarding his past causes: 'I always mindfully recollect the Buddha and delight in seeing him.'"
World-Honored One, he constantly makes vows never to be separated from the Buddha-sun. Thus we know that his manifestation of great expedient power is subtle, wondrous, and inconceivable;
he protects sentient beings and manifests his body to bring them benefit. Therefore, the praises of his merits found in the various sutras are truly immeasurable.

Hārītī, the Joyful Mother Hārītī—whose name in the language of China means "Evil Thief. Formerly, on a mountain within the city of Rājagṛha in Central India, there was a yakṣa named Sata who protected the people.
Not long after he had taken a wife from among his own kind, a daughter was born to them.
The youth’s appearance was dignified and handsome, and he possessed a great variety of medicinal herbs; seeing this, everyone rejoiced, and thus he was named "Joy" (Huanxi).
As he gradually grew older, there was at that time in the kingdom of Gandhāra in Northern India a yakṣa named Pañcika (also called Cchagala).

He took Prahlāda as his wife. Because she had previously been a cowherd girl who offered five hundred *āmra* fruits to a pratyekabuddha while making an evil vow, she would say to her husband every time:
"I wish to take and eat all the sons and daughters born in the city of Rājagṛha. Although her husband repeatedly forbade her, she later gave birth to five hundred sons. At that point...
The son was named Priyaputra (“Beloved Son”) and the daughter was named Śrīdevī (“Goddess of Fortune”). Relying on the power of her son, she did not heed her husband’s admonitions.
She would seize and eat any children born to people. The king and his ministers were struck with alarm and wonder, yet the calamity could not be averted through sacrifices.
Then, the tutelary deity of the city appeared in a dream and told the people: “All of your sons and daughters are being devoured by the yakṣa Priya.”
The people replied, "One who eats our sons and daughters is an evil thief; how can he be called 'Joyful'? For this reason, she was named Hārītī.
Then the people all went to the Buddha’s dwelling to seek her subjugation. The Buddha covered her beloved child with his alms-bowl;
she beat her breast and wept in grief, searching for him throughout heaven and earth, but could not find him anywhere. [She then sought] the Great Learned One (Mahāśravaṇa).
"O Heavenly King, instruct him to take refuge in the World-Honored One. Let the Buddha cause him to receive the precepts and bestow fearlessness upon others.
Following the Buddha’s instruction, he will immediately see his beloved son. The Buddha will preach the Dharma for him, and he will subsequently realize the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Furthermore, summon his sons to likewise rely on the Buddha's precepts and not harass the people. In the kitchens of monasteries in the Western Regions, images of this deity are frequently enshrined.
Their food and drink were abundant and without lack. For those ordinary people who had no offspring, they sought her and obtained children;
for those with illnesses, they prayed to her and were restored to peace. Her five hundred sons all became spirit-kings, commanding a multitude of ten thousand ghosts;
therefore, she is also called the Mother of the Ghost Kings.
Mārīcī-devī, Mārīcī.
In the language of China, this means "mirage" (yángyàn). Because her form and characteristics cannot be seen and cannot be grasped, she is like a mirage.
She protects the state and the people, and rescues them from calamities such as warfare. The Buddha said: "The goddess Mārīcī possesses great [power]..."
Possessing supernormal powers, she always walks before the sun; the sun does not see her, yet she can see the sun.
No one can see her, no one can know her, and no one can seize or harm her; she is not even afraid of enemies.
If there is anyone who knows the name of this Goddess Mārīcī, that person likewise cannot be seen, nor can they be harmed by enemies.
Then, that celestial maiden bends her left arm upward, forming a fist with her wrist positioned in front of her left breast.
Within the fist, she holds a celestial fan. The fan is like that of Vimalakīrti; as the maiden holds the fan, in its center she forms a *svastika* (卍) of the Western regions.
Inside each of the four curves of the character, she places the shape of four suns, one upon the other. Such is the fan.
Above, form the shape of a flame. Extend the right arm and stretch out all five fingers, with the fingertips pointing downward.
If one follows the ritual procedure according to the sūtra and recites the mantra of that deity, there will be great spiritual resonance; its supernatural power is inconceivable.
The city walls of the Devaputra Sūryagātraprabha are made of celestial golden crystal. They are fifty-one yojanas in length and breadth, square like a residence, appearing round from a distance.
The palaces are composed of a hundred jewels, and the litters and carriages are made of purple gold, sixteen [yojanas] in height.
In a distance of one yojana, the devaputra and his retinue experience subtle and exquisite pleasures therein. The city walls, palaces, and carriages all possess one thousand rays of light:
five hundred shine sideways and five hundred shine downward. Five winds sustain and cause them to revolve.
It travels around Mount Sumeru and further illuminates the four continents, dispelling the gloom and destroying the darkness, bringing all things to maturity.
This deity was originally born there because he practiced generosity, cultivated goodness, and served the Buddha. He shares the same lifespan as the Four Heavenly Kings, which is five hundred years;
his descendants succeed one another, and they dwell together for one kalpa. Separately, there are immeasurable other deities who reside within the sun.
They proceeded before the palace, each enjoying celestial music. "Jewel Radiance" (*Ratnaprabhā*) is its name. The new sutra says:
"When the sun rises, it emits a thousand rays; its stainless flames are pure. By the power of this King of Sutras, its radiance flows and encircles the four continents.
By the majestic power of this sutra, it assists the Son of Heaven. When the sunlight shines upon this Jambudvīpa, the fields..."
All medicinal fruits are made to ripen well, filling the great earth. [There are] five winds: first, the sustaining wind;

second, the nourishing wind; third, the receiving wind; fourth, the transforming wind; and fifth, the regulating wind. One kalpa refers to one intermediate kalpa (antarakalpa), which consists of twenty minor kalpas (kṣudrakalpa).
The city-walls of the Moon Palace of the Moon-God King are composed of celestial silver and blue lapis lazuli; they are forty-nine yojanas in length and breadth.
The palace is composed of a hundred jewels, and the great carriage is made of blue lapis lazuli, sixteen yojanas in height. The King and his [retinue]...
Together with their retinues, they experience subtle and wondrous bliss therein. Their cities, palaces, and carriages possess a thousand rays of light:

five hundred shine sideways and five hundred shine downward. Five winds sustain and carry them as they travel around the midsection of Mount Sumeru, illuminating the four continents and nourishing all things in the shade, thereby benefiting and delivering sentient beings. This is due to the wholesome karma cultivated through their past causes.
The Root is also equal to the Sun Deity; his lifespan is five hundred years, and his descendants succeed one another, dwelling together for an entire kalpa.
There are also immeasurable celestial palaces that precede the Moon Palace, where they constantly experience bliss. This is the Bright Moon.
As for their names:
the Buddha Mahāvidyut-rāja said, "In the east there is the Vidyut-rāja of Radiance named Ajita; in the south there is the Vidyut-rāja of Radiance..."
The king is named Śatru. In the western direction there is a lightning-lightning king named Bahuprabha;
in the northern direction there is a lightning-lightning king named Sūtamani. If a person hears the names of such lightning kings as these, [they shall attain protection].
Furthermore, one who knows the names of the directional guardians will immediately be far removed from all matters of fear and all calamities;

they shall all be completely extinguished. If one writes down the names of these four directional Lightning Kings at one's dwelling place, there will be no fear of thunder and lightning, nor any misfortunes, obstacles, afflictions, or untimely, wrongful deaths; all such things will be entirely kept at a distance.
Sāgara Anavatapta Nāgarāja,
"Sāgara" being the Chinese translation for "Salt Ocean," derives its name from the sea.
He is the seventh among the one hundred and seventy-seven nāga kings within that Salt Ocean, and is a great powerful bodhisattva of the tenth stage manifesting as a nāga.
As soon as the King’s body raised his thought, dense clouds spread forth and sweet rain poured down, universally moistening the world beneath heaven. He protected the Dharma and the people;
his benefits were vast and extensive. As the Sūtra says: "In the midst of the great ocean, ten thousand *yojanas* deep, there is a city named Kṣemavatī (Playful Joy).
It is three thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth. Its walls and towers are composed of the seven treasures, and it contains various flower ponds, flowing streams, and groves."
The gardens were adorned with necklaces of jewels. Within the palaces were four precious gems capable of producing all manner of rare treasures within the ocean.
The palace of the dragon king’s son, Yāpī-dhvaja, and the palaces of eight billion great dragon kings were each distinct from one another.
From within these dragon kings’ palaces, water of a deep lapis lazuli color issued forth.
The ocean surges forth at its appointed time; therefore, the tides of the great sea do not miss their season. Its splendor is no different from that of the heavens.
In the Sanskrit language it is called Anavatapta, which in the language of China means "Free from Heat and Affliction. It derives its name from the lake.

This Dragon King is also a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), who dwells upon the summit of the Snowy Mountains by the Lake Anavatapta in a hall made of the seven treasures and supported by five pillars.
They produce cool, clear water to provide for Jambudvīpa and to benefit and deliver sentient beings.
At that time, together with twenty-eight thousand nāga kings, they proceeded to the assembly of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*. The new translation states:
Anavatapta, Sāgara, Mucilinda, Elāpattra, Nanda, and Upananda—among the ten thousand nāgas, these possess supernatural powers and majestic virtue, and together they provide protection.
The person who upholds this sutra shall never be parted from them day or night.
The Yakṣa King Padmavaktra—
yakṣa being a transliteration of *yakṣa*, which in the language of China means "valiant and strong," or "fierce and evil," or again, "noble person"— is able to...
Soaring through the air, there are three kinds [of yakṣas]: first, those on the earth; second, those in the void; and third, those who guard the cities and moats in the two lower heavens.

The one named Padmavaktra (Lotus Face), together with thirty-six thousand yakṣas, all delight in the Tathāgata’s True Dharma and protect it with profound resolve, never giving rise to weariness or indolence. They have gathered at the Golden Light.
The *Minghui* (Explanatory Commentary) states that the new scripture says: "The Yakṣa Kings Ratnarāja, Pūrṇabhadra, Kāntāraka,
and Kumbhīra, as well as Piṅgala— these Yakṣa Kings, each with a retinue of five hundred— shall all come to collectively protect those who see and hear this sutra."

The Gandharva King Citrasena—*gandharva* being translated into Chinese as "fragrance-body" (*xiāngyīn*)—is a celestial musician deity who does not consume wine or meat, but sustains his body solely by smelling fragrances.
He dwells in the Vajra Cave on the southern side of Mount Sumeru. "Citrasena" is his name; he has profound faith in the Mahāyāna.
Together with the hosts of gandharvas, they protect the sutras and protect the people,
causing the Buddha-dharma to circulate. Vemacitra, the asura king—
*asura* being translated in the vernacular as "non-deva"— because his karmic retribution is most excellent, he ranks next to the various devas, yet he is not [a deva].

The Heaven (deva) is one of the six realms of existence (*ṣadgati*). The males are ugly while the females are handsome. There are the realm of ghosts (*preta*) and the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*).
The ghosts dwell in caves on Mount Sumeru or along the shores of the great ocean; the animals dwell at the bottom of the great ocean. There are four modes of birth:
viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, and transformation-born. Vemacitra dwells at the bottom of the great ocean, one thousand *yojana* to the east of Mount Sumeru.
The land is forty thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Within the great city, the palace is named Śvetaketu;
it is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold rows of trees.
The palaces and gardens are all composed of the seven precious substances, adorned and embellished beyond description. To the south and west of Mount Sumeru...
To the north, each extending for more than a thousand yojanas beneath the great ocean, there are respective cities and kingdoms of asuras.
Their natural bodies are seven hundred yojanas in height, while their transformation bodies are sixteen thousand eight hundred yojanas tall; they stand thus at the bottom of the great ocean.
He was equal in height to Mount Sumeru and constantly fought with the gods. When defeated, he would hide his army within the fibers of a lotus stalk.
Vemacitra is his name; Vemacitra means "High Resonance," also "Pure Mind," and is further called "Various Doubts.
He married the Gandharva daughter of Mount Gandhamādana and fathered Śacī, whom Śakra took as his wife.
Śacī was his chief consort. Vemacitra’s retinue and power were beyond measure;
the rest of his ministers, attendants, and servants were likewise incalculable. Food and clothing appeared spontaneously, with a hundred flavors appearing at will, equal to those of the gods.
Their garments, crowns, and neck-ribbons were made of pure seven-jewels, fresh and clean. He vowed to protect the True Dharma.
The Dharma. To protect and uphold this sutra, they attend the assembly of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*. The new translation states:
"Vajra, Rāhu, Vemacitrin, Mucilinda, Kumbhīra, Mahābāhu, and Nandika, together with countless hosts of devas, come to protect those who uphold this sutra.
The *Huayan Yingyan Ji* (Record of Miraculous Responses of the Avataṃsaka) states: "In the kingdom of Khotan, there was a śrāmaṇera named Prajñā..."

Migabao strictly maintained his precepts and devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. One day, a person suddenly appeared before him with palms joined and said, "The devas invite you;

I pray that you close your eyes. In an instant, they arrived in the heavens. The Heavenly Emperor knelt and entreated him, saying, "We are currently at war with the asuras and have repeatedly been defeated.
We humbly request that you recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for us, hoping for the Dharma [to prevail]."
Through the empowerment of his spiritual power, the Master ascended a celestial chariot and focused his mind upon the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

As the hosts of devas confronted the formidable enemy, the asuras suddenly broke and scattered. In an instant, he was escorted back home, his body suffused with celestial fragrance that did not fade for the rest of his life.
The Sura Garuḍa King—*garuḍa* in Sanskrit, *jīnqì* (Golden Wing) in Chinese—has golden-colored wings adorned with various colors.
The distance between his two wings is three hundred and sixty *li*, and there are also instances where it is one hundred and sixty thousand *li*. From head to tail...
It travels a thousand *yojanas*, and its height and depth are likewise the same. It has a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) upon its neck and takes dragons as its food;
however, it cannot eat those dragons who have received the Three Refuges and the Eight Precepts. Its name is Sura;

it possesses the greatest supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and deeply delights in the Mahāyāna sūtras, attending the assembly of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*. The *Āgama* sūtras state that this bird has four modes of birth (*catasro yonayaḥ*).
They wear necklaces made of wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*). They manifest ten thousand transformations, accomplishing everything without exception.
Their bodies are forty *li* tall; their robes are eighty *li* wide and forty *li* long. Their lifespan is one *kalpa*. Some are even more [distinguished].
This is not the king of birds. On the northern shore of the great ocean, there is a great tree named Kūṭaśālmali, one hundred yojanas in height and fifty yojanas in circumference.
Birds dwell within it. On the four sides of the tree are birds born from the four modes of birth—womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born.
The feathers of these birds are poisonous; when they flap their wings, the wind enters the eyes of humans and causes blindness. Therefore...
They do not come among humans. They stand upon iron trees at the edge of Mount Sumeru.

As for the Gandharva kings and Gandharvas—whose name translates in the language of China as "Doubtful Spirits"—they resemble humans but have horns upon their heads; when people see them, they call them humans.
"Is he a human? Or is he a non-human? Because of this, he was given a name.
He is a divine musician of the Heavenly Emperor, who also attended the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* assembly together with his retinue. The new translation states:
"The Kinnara music gods, the Sura and Garuḍa kings, Mahāprajñā, and Śrī—these and other leading devas each lead their respective celestial hosts and constantly make offerings."
They nourish all Buddhas and the inconceivable Dharma-treasure, constantly giving rise to a heart of joy and maintaining reverence for the sutras.
The King of the Mahoragas (the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that King Mahāsudarśana was their leader) is also called a Māhāraka;
in the Chinese language, this means "large-bellied crawler," referring to the terrestrial dragons. They, too, together with their retinues...
He attended the assembly of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.

Yama-raja is called *Yama* in Sanskrit; in the language of China, it means "Twin Kings," referring to the fact that both the elder brother and the younger sister serve as lords of the hells. The elder brother...

The elder brother governs the affairs of men; the younger sister governs the affairs of women; hence they are called the "Twin Kings" (*yamaka-rāja*). They are also called "Quellers of Strife," meaning they bring to rest the disputes of those who have committed offenses.
A sutra states that five hundred *yojanas* beneath Jambudvīpa lies the city of King Yama, with its four sides extending seventy-five thousand *yojanas*.
It is further said that he dwells in the city situated between the hells, measuring thirty thousand [yojanas] in length and breadth.

Around the four sides of the city, various hells are arrayed. Some say these were created as transformations by a Bodhisattva for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, who presides over the dark realm.
In the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, King Yama speaks a verse to the sinners, saying:
"You have obtained a human body but did not cultivate the Way; it is like entering a mountain of jewels and returning empty-handed."
"You have now created this for yourself and must now experience it for yourself. What can you do by crying out in suffering? The *Daśarājaka-sūtra* states:

"King Yama shall become a Buddha in a future age, titled Tathāgata Universal King (*Samantaprabha-rāja*), and together with his retinue, he will attend the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* assembly to protect those who uphold this sūtra. The new sūtra states: "The Sun and Moon Devas, Śakra, the Wind [Deva]..."
The deities of water and fire, Vaisravana, Mahābhuja, Yama, Pratibhāna, and all the World-Protectors—
valiant and endowed with majestic power— shall protect those who uphold this sutra, never departing from them by day or night.
Whenever making offerings during a vegetarian feast, recite the *bhojya-pariṇāmana-mantra* twenty-one times. Within this mantra, three characters are in the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

The character *vā* should be pronounced with the sound "fa" (伐); alternatively, the character *bhā* may be pronounced with the entering tone (*rùshēng*). By no means should it be pronounced as the character "fǔ" (阜).
The syllable *ra* should be recited with the sound of the two syllables *la-la*; by no means should it be recited as the syllable *lai*.
The syllable *oṃ* is uttered with a raised tone from the throat. The syllable *hūṃ* is called with the mouth closed, the sound emerging from the chest and throat like the bellowing of an ox;
alternatively, it may be pronounced as *hoṃ* or as *huṃ* (a conjunct). Currently, there are those in the monastic courts who perform human-oriented ritual ceremonies (*mānuṣya-dharma*).

They have arbitrarily added phrases such as "sending [the deities] back to heaven. However, within the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* Repentance Ritual (*Jin guangming chanfa*), there is originally no text for "sending";

likewise, even in the *Mahākaruṇā* Repentance Ritual, there is an invitation but no sending. One must not arbitrarily add such elements to contravene the intent of the scriptures. Furthermore, they increase various kinds of nasal chanting (*nanchang*) to disturb the ears of the deities;
with a lack of single-minded sincerity and an intent focused merely on singing and chanting, there will certainly be no spiritual resonance, and it will ultimately result in emptiness.
